speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The LBC is a tax on the increase in land value, resulting from a chargeable consent given in relation to the land, on or after the Bill’s operative date.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It ensures the return to the community, as set out in section 5 of the Bill, of an appropriate proportion of economic benefits from the grant of rights to develop or otherwise use land.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The money collected as LBC can then be used to fund a wide range of infrastructure development and public programmes undertaken by the Government.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Today, there is already an existing framework by which Development Charge, which I shall call DC, or Temporary Development Levy, which I shall call TDL, is collected by URA and a Differential Premium, a DP, which is collected by the Singapore Land Authority (SLA) today.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Those three charges are similar in nature, as they all cream-off in different ways the increase in value of land resulting from chargeable consents.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The principles for computing LBC and proposed rates of charging will remain largely unchanged from the current regime.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will benefit landowners and developers, as they no longer need to apply to various public sector agencies for the payment of such charges.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Part 2 of the Bill sets out the tax rate and rules for calculating the LBC.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These should already be familiar to landowners and developers as they are currently used by URA and SLA in calculating DP, TDL and DC.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Bill itself does not set out the tax rate, which is a percentage of the increase in the value of the land likely to accrue from the giving of the chargeable consent.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The rate itself will be set out by the Minister in regulations and will be reviewed periodically as necessary.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In certain cases, as Members may know, on an exceptional basis, the LBC rate will be higher – that is also the case today – based on 100% of the increase in land value.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, where the state title contains a restrictive covenant on change of land use because the land was previously sold by the state directly to the lessee without a tender.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The current practice is to collect DP at 100% of the enhancement of land value, if there were to be a material change of use of that piece of land.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Second, where the state title contains an “additional land premium” condition.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Such a condition may be included in a state title to allow for the collection of the value enhancement arising from an intensification or change of use of land, prior to a certain cut-off date, such as before the Temporary Occupation Permit (TOP) of a development is obtained, or until certain conditions are met.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The condition is to discourage landowners from changing their plans shortly after the purchase of the piece of land from the state, in order to avoid paying the full market rate to the state at the point of purchase.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These methods are, again, not dissimilar to how DC, TDL and DP are computed today.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The first method uses a Table of Rates, which is similar to the DC Table of Rates in the Planning (Development Charges) Rules today, which goes by each geographic sector and land use group.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Table of Rates will apply for the majority of cases and will allow landowners to estimate the amount of LBC upfront using that Table of Rates.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This provides a clear and certain process for landowners and developers to assess the likely LBC that they would have to pay should they choose to enhance or develop the use of land.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The second method involves a valuation of the enhancement in land value by the Chief Valuer of the Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS) or a private valuer appointed by SLA.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The second method applies where a taxable person chooses this method in lieu of using the Table of Rates method; or in specific circumstances where the Table of Rates might be inapplicable, such as where there is either no suitable or no comparable use group for assessment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Table of Rates and formulae for computing LBC will be prescribed in the Regulations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These will adhere with current principles, except for an adjustment for leasehold properties which will be standardised under the LBC regime.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In other words, the adjustment is made depending on the length of the balance of the remnant lease.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: There is currently no such adjustment for DC today to take into account the remaining tenure.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, this adjustment would make for a more accurate reflection of value.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Part 3 of the Bill sets out the provisions to exempt or provide concessionary relief from the liability to pay LBC.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Specifically, clause 13 empowers the Minister for National Development, in consultation with the Minister for Law, to provide for concessionary relief from the payment of LBC.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will allow MND to make provisions for concessionary relief in certain circumstances such as meeting planning objectives – for instance to encourage conservation of certain properties, or the comprehensive redevelopment of multiple private properties for more optimal use of land; or to encourage construction productivity; or to promote environmentally sustainable development.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will enable the continuation of existing DC exemptions which are provided for under the Planning Act today.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, the regime for concessions exists today, in the Planning Act.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It will also provide the Government with flexibility to extend concessionary relief in future to encourage desired outcomes on land planning and development.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Deferment of LBC liability is discretionary and not automatic.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This, I should add to Members, is also similar to what is currently provided for in the Planning (Deferment of Payment of Development Charge by Charities) Rules 2017, and in the Planning (Deferment of Payment of Temporary Development Levy by Charities) Rules 2016.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Where two or more persons may have a material interest in the land or are joint owners of a material interest, the Bill requires SLA to apportion the liability.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Part 5 of the Bill deals with assessment and collection of the LBC, while Part 6 of the Bill deals with the recovery of unpaid LBC.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: What is new is SLA is empowered to issue a rectification order to collect penalty tax on top of the LBC due, where there has been an illegal development of land, and URA regularises the development through a subsequent planning authorisation afterwards; or where there is an activity, development or subdivision carried out in breach of a restrictive covenant contained in a state title, and SLA assesses that it is not reasonably practicable or it is undesirable to stop or resume any controlled activity or to reinstate the land.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To give Members an example of when this might happen – a developer may have subdivided the land and sold them to multiple buyers, and it would not be reasonably practicable or desirable in such a situation to order reinstatement.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: SLA will also be given the discretion to impose a higher or lower penalty tax at a percentage fixed by the Bill – to increase the penalty tax if the taxpayer hinders or obstructs the determination of the taxpayer’s liability; or to reduce the amount of penalty tax where the defaulting taxpayer is cooperative.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will simplify the process of collection and provide greater transparency for landowners and developers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: With that, Mr Speaker, I beg to move.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As a matter of public interest, land here – those pieces that we have agreed to be developed – should be developed to its optimal potential.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Where the Government allows for land to be developed more optimally, its value, in most circumstances, will tend to increase.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This Bill deals with the increased value arising from consent on the part of the public authorities.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The logic of this is that the value created by the decision of a public body must benefit the public.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: To share the increase in the value of land with the public is not a new concept.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Since Independence in 1965, Singapore has a Development Charge (DC) system, as mentioned by the hon Minister, under the Planning Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is a tax that is payable when planning permission is granted to carry out development projects that increases the allowable intensity or allows a change in zoning that increase the value of land.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Singapore also has a Development Premium (DP) system which works similarly.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is an elegant solution to consolidate the bases for taxation and the levying of a charge arising from increase in land value because a public authority agrees to lift restrictions to enable a better utility of the land.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There are similar pieces of legislation in many parts of the world, including the United Kingdom.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I seek some clarifications on the Bill with a view to understand the scope of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For example, when dealing with remnant land which is not capable of independent development because of the small size or shape, but has amalgamation potential which can bring out an enhancement in land value.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What will be the situation where the planning authority allows for amalgamation of land plots that has the effect of increasing the land value of the remnant land?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: From my perusal of what constitutes “chargeable consent” under the Bill, such situations seem to fall outside the Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In contrast, a Land Betterment Charge may be levied arising from chargeable consent given in relation to sub-division of any land, even if there is no development on it, giving rise to an increase in its land value.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Also, may I clarify that the Government will continue with the current practice to charge DP in such situations?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Second, I would like to understand the applicability of the Bill vis-à-vis decisions of the Court that may have the effect of enhancing land value.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Let us take an example where the Court makes a declaration that the burden of an easement over a servient tenement has been abandoned.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As a consequence, the land value of the servient tenement may increase.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Or, alternatively, a situation where the Court exercises the power under section 105A or section 140(5) of the Land Titles Act to vary or extinguish an easement or restriction over a servient tenement on the basis that they are obsolete and such burdens impede the development of the land.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In such situations, by a stroke of the pen of the judge, the land value may increase too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Again, my reading of the definition of "chargeable consent" is that such situations fall outside the Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In my respectful view, if my reading is correct, there is little difference between an administrator lifting a restriction and the Court lifting a restriction that results in an increase in land value.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Alternatively, we should separately capture part of the increased value arising from Court decisions for public good.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In Singapore, land is a vehicle through which Singaporeans' wealth is built and transmitted.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is our duty to ensure that we make the best rules possible to optimise its use and to distribute the gains fairly.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I believe the Bill represents a step in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I look forward to the Minister's responses to my points of clarification.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I shall try to read my speech as quickly as I can.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: My parliamentary colleague, Mr Louis Chua will make an important speech, situating this Bill in the context of the Government's overall stance towards land sales in the treatment of the various revenue streams it thereby gains.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: While I support this Bill, I will focus my speech here today on three broad areas which are mostly technical and clarificatory: firstly, greater transparency on information and consultation on this new Land Betterment Charge Bill; secondly, issues around concessionary relief in deferment of liability to pay, ensuring that we give incentives only to developments that are rightly and squarely in the public interest; and thirdly, technical clarifications of interest to industry stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: By streamlining and combining these three charges into a single charge, this could simplify the processes for stakeholders and iron out any earlier disputes of unfairness in the different calculation methods for the different charges.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: However, to unlock these benefits, there should be greater transparency, accountability and stakeholder consultation on how this new Land Betterment Charge regime actually works.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Under clause 65 of the Bill, the Minister may make regulations to use the Table of Rates method.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: While we understand that the exact regulations will only be available at a later date, may I clarify broadly how the Land Betterment Charges will be calculated in relation to the existing regime of calculations of Development Charges, Temporary Development Levy (TDL) and Differential Premium.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Will it have elements of the existing regime or will it be a wholly new system?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Will there be greater alignment across existing regimes?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: My colleague, Mr Louis Chua will pose similar questions in his speech.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Has there been a public consultation conducted on these changes?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: If yes, can the Ministry make public the results of the same, and if not, will the Ministry conduct one at some stage?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For legislation as nuanced as this, it would be beneficial to seek out a range of stakeholder feedback.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We need to surface and address potential issues and pitfalls with stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In case studies from other countries such as Australia and the UK, policy experts and think tanks have noted the complexity of land value capture taxation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For example, while the UK has had a long history of land value capture, it has been of limited success.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This was partially due to local authorities being burdened with the implementation of the policy without the necessary resources.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, Sir, clause 10(2) of the LBC Bill allows for not just the chief valuer but also "another individual pointed by the authority to ascertain the amount of land betterment charge by the valuation method." This opens up questions around the possibility of bias and quality control.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This may erode trust and support within the industry for the new regime.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Will only one valuation by a single third party be allowed?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Will the chief valuer have the final say?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In other words, what controls will be introduced to check on the work of third party valuers under this Bill in respect of quality and the possibility of bias?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In many countries, similar charges are used to fund new or pay off existing infrastructure projects in the communities where the charges are collected.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For example, the construction of Hong Kong's metro railway was funded solely from the sale of development rights around stations.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Close to one-third of London's Crossrail is being funded by levies on nearby businesses.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: How will the funds collected by the new LBC be used to return benefits to the community?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Will these funds be earmarked for infrastructural works, for example?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: My parliamentary colleague, Mr Louis Chua, will make a similar point and ask for greater clarity around this as well.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We want to incentivise only developments that advance the public interest.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Could the Government provide concrete examples of the kinds of developments that would be eligible?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: What are the criteria for determining the eligibility for this relief?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: What are the guiding principles and what are the factors taken into consideration for determining the quantum of relief?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Right now, under clause 13(1), the "Land Planning Minister may, after consulting the Minister, provide by order in the Gazette for concessionary relief" of the Land Betterment Charge.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In the case of competing interests, how will decisions be made?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For example, in the cases of Mandai Park developments in the Cross Island Line, these developments may result in economic benefits but they carry potential adverse environmental impacts.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Also, can the Government give itself concessionary relief?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This appears to be the case from current rules.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: If so, how is the potential for conflict of interest managed?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Can agencies and Statutory Boards seek concessionary relief and appeal decisions if concessionary relief is not obtained, and, if so, who hears such appeals?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Beyond environmental sustainability, which is mentioned in the Bill, I would like to encourage concessionary relief to be granted on the grounds of other public interest such as the conservation of heritage and art spaces.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This was a good use of the flexibility of the DC policy tool to incentivise developers to come on board and ensure the conserved building remains economically viable.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: A conservation expert Prof Yeo Kang Shua has termed these incentives as "unprecedented and signalling that the costs of revitalisation are reduced or subsidised by the state to safeguard the common good of the country's architectural heritage".

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Does the LBC include such flexibility as well?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: What the Government consider providing such planning incentives to development proposals for other heritage buildings?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, clause 22A provides for a deferment to be made if "the taxable person is a charitable institution and the land will be used wholly or mainly for charitable purposes whether of the taxable person or that person in other charitable institutions".

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This is a positive step and will help offset the costs of running charities so that more of their resources can be channelled towards worthy causes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: However, I have a few clarifications to seek.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There may be organisations that have IPC status and work for the public good but are officially not registered as a charity, but as a society, for example.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: With annual funding at the time of less than $70,000 from Sport Singapore and annual rental estimated at $72,000 for the Jubilee Industrial Building space, they were unable to pay the TDL.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: They had appealed URA's decision but did not succeed.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: However, earlier in 2009, the SWF had successfully applied for a waiver of the TDL when it moved from Mountbatten Community Club to Kallang.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But this time, their request was rejected in 2015.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: At that time, the weightlifting community was worried about the future of their sport in the country, given rising costs and these sorts of impediments.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We ought to protect the future of sports in Singapore along with other worthy causes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, I would like to raise some points for technical clarification.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: If leviable, how do we reconcile this with the general position that tax is not levied on payments of tax or, in other words, that there should be no tax on tax?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Under the current regime, stamp duty is leviable on DP and paid to the relevant authorities when enhancing or intensifying the use of land.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, on renewal of state leases and the definition of chargeable consent.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Clause 3 of the Bill does not appear to capture the renewal of the leasehold tenure of state leases, for example, a 99-year lease.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It is not clear as to whether or not the LBC applies to renewals.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Hence, I would like to seek clarification on this point.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, under the current regime, the DP is typically only payable on the acceptance of the offer made by the relevant competent authorities with regard to the proposed enhancement of a land parcel.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The proposed enhancement is formalised by way of a contractual agreement between the developer and the relevant competent authority, for example, SLA, by way of an offer made by the competent authority in the acceptance of the terms thereof by the developer – for example, Differential Premium payable, deadline for acceptance of the offer and so on.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: As part of the terms, Differential Premiums are typically required to be paid on acceptance of the offer.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: When a case of proposed enhancement is raised under the LBC, it seems that a liability order will be issued by the SLA after one of the following dates: firstly, the date that a planning permission or conservation permission, as the case may be, is granted in respect of the development of the land; and secondly, the date where the competent authority or land planning Minister notifies SLA that the competent authority or the land planning Minister, as the case may be, intends to grant final permission under clause 17(4) of the Planning Act 1998.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This means that the payment of LBC could be at an earlier stage than DP under the current regime since for DP, the offer and acceptance happens months after the grant of planning permission is issued.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It is not clear at what stage under the proposed regime would the applicant become aware of the different conditions they would be subjected to as the offer is being made and whether or not they would be able to refuse, reject or discontinue the proposed development after being granted provisional permission, planning permission or conservation permission.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, will SLA introduce guidelines or a requirement that all changes of use applications include an undertaking that the LBC has been discussed between landlord and tenant?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: While this is a good step, it would be helpful to have guidelines or a requirement that the landlord and tenant discussed this.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Anecdotal evidence suggests that in certain cases in the past, the tenant was made to bear the cost of TDL although the landlord also benefited from the change in land use permission by way of charging higher rents to the tenant.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Can there be more specific criteria that would render a business immediately eligible for such deferment?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It would be helpful if the criteria on which these decisions would be made are spelt out more clearly.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: If businesses are unable to pay the TDL, they might have to close down, leading to losses to themselves, their landlords and their employees.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The Government will also lose out on tax revenue.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Can URA consider giving such businesses rebates or deferments on their TDL?" That concludes my speech.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As such, it is equitable that such economic benefits are returned to the community.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have three points of clarification on this Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first point is on the mechanisms in place to ensure that the planning objectives of the Bill are achieved.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These conditions include that the relief will lead to a more optimal use of land, improve the productivity of the construction sector and promote environmentally sustainable development of land.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These objectives are wide-ranging and very general in nature.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Given how broad these objectives are, can the Minister explain which of these specific planning objectives the concessionary relief granted to a development is intended to achieve?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister also explain how he envisions the development will achieve the intended planning objectives?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Additionally, given that a fairly long timeframe may be required to determine if some of these objectives are achieved, what measures are in place to track whether concessionary relief granted achieved the intended planning objectives?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In contrast to the Land Planning Minister's power to provide concessionary relief, the Minister's power to grant a general exemption is not expressly limited by any planning objectives.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister provide assurance that the Minister's power will be exercised in line with the purpose of the Act as set out under the new section 5?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In other words, will Minister's power to grant general exemptions be consistent with the objectives of urban development, enhance productivity for the construction industry and promote environmentally sustainable development?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third point is how the Government will recover benefits from any unlawful development.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, even if an unauthorised activity ceases or the land restored, the developer may still have reaped benefits for the period that the unlawful development lasted.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can Minister clarify what powers the Ministry has to require that a developer disgorge the benefits that it has reaped from such unlawful development?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Before I begin, Mr Speaker, I would like to declare my interest as a research analyst covering the real estate sector.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is notwithstanding, of course, that Singapore's land area stands at around 276 square kilometres as at 2019, about 140 square kilometres or 24% higher than what it was 50 years ago.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: After all, there is a hard limit to the amount of land reclamation that can be carried out in our waters.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It is thus essential that we focus on optimising Singapore's land use so as to extract the maximum socio-economic benefits for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Optimising land use has come a long way in Singapore, starting with the amendment of the Land Acquisition Act in 1966, following Singapore's Independence.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Back in 1964, then Prime Minister Mr Lee Kuan Yew shared two broad principles on land acquisition.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The first is that no private landowners should benefit from development which has taken place at public expense; and, second, prices paid on acquisition for public purposes should not be higher than what the land would have been worth had the Government not contemplated development generally in that area.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: With these principles in mind, the Land Acquisition Act was subsequently amended to strengthen the Government's powers to acquire land and limit compensation.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In the debate on the Land Acquisition Bill, Mr EW Barker, then Minister for Law and National Development, concluded that: "There has not been a word of criticism.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I have nothing much to add except to say that I am glad that our backbenchers have realised the importance and the necessity for this piece of socialist legislation." The Land Acquisition Act has since been amended given changing circumstances, with the 2007 amendment providing for compensation based on prevailing market value of acquired land.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Effectively, the Government has become the largest landowner and landlord, with the ability to simultaneously influence both demand and supply through policy levers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Critically, the Government also has the ability to extract monetary value from land throughout the course of time, with land having characteristics of a renewable resource and not a finite one.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: First, I stand corrected, but it is the policy of this Government that, for leasehold land sold, at the end of the land lease tenure, land will revert to the Government for free and will thus be available for sale once again.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Second, stamp duties will provide for taxes to be collected when sale or rental transactions occur.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Thirdly, property taxes are collected on an annual basis.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For example, what used to be a low-rise carpark and hawker centre in the heart of the CBD, are set to be transformed into a modern mixed-use commercial complex rising to a height of 280 metres, one of the tallest buildings in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While the size of the land plot has not changed, the implied land value has soared considerably.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The LBC will thus be a logical policy lever to allow for value captured by the state for the public good.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The streamlining of legislation and easing of administrative burden would just be much appreciated by private developers and public officers alike.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: That said, I do have a number of specific clarifications to raise on the LBC.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Clause 9 sets out the two methods to be used in assessing the amount of LBC – the Table of Rates method and the evaluation by designated valuers method.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Today, DC rates are reviewed on a half-yearly basis in consultation with the Chief Valuer.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Can the Minister clarify how the Table of Rates will be assessed and how will it be different from the current DC regime?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: How much will DC collections on an annual basis in the past and how would this differ with the switch to an LBC mechanism?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Conceptually, almost all developments benefit from existing amenities and infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: So, it is also fair that those who benefit financially when planning permission is given should share some of their gain with the community.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, it is also difficult to quantify the land value increment resulting from infrastructure investments.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Revaluation being a subjective matter, how would, for example, aggrieved landowners seek recourse for any disagreements in land valuation and LBCs, whether it is assessed under the table of rates method or the valuation method.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Second, with the blurring of lines across use groups and greater creativity in land use optimisation, we are already seeing retail malls of today house co-working offices while it is increasingly common to have lifestyle in hospitality provisions, in Grade A office buildings.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: How will SLA ensure that its table of rates is a dynamic one and not based on static singular interpretations of land use?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Third, on the powers conferred on the Minister.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Clause 12 confers powers on the Minister to exempt any person or class of persons from all or any of the provisions of the Bill either generally or in a particular case and subject to such conditions as the Minister may impose.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: How is this exercise of legislative powers safeguarded and what would the conditions entail?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Have similar exemptions been exercised in the past and what were the circumstances behind it back then?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In practical terms, who will be the land planning Minister and would not the conditions under subsection 2(a), (b) and (c) be desirable, loosely defined conditions that we will expect out of property development in Singapore regardless?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Aside from the Act, these include the desirability of the proposed development or subdivision of any land in achieving economic development or maintaining the cultural, economic, physical and social well-being of the people of Singapore and the community in the area concerned.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While this would simplify recovery efforts, is such a clause fair to the tenants and should not efforts be focused on the defaulting party instead?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Clause 5 sets out admirable causes for imposing an LBC, including amongst others, ensuring the return to the community of an appropriate proportion of economic benefits from the grant of rights to develop or otherwise use land and to promote or encourage environmentally sustainable development or use of land.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Would the Land Betterment Charges collected from the development be earmarked for the specific community in question?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And how would SLA enforce the requirement for environmentally sustainable development?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The basis for payment computations will remain the same.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Hence, as I understand it, the changes serve primarily to simplify the process for payment computations and to consolidate collections under SLA.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: At the same time, the tax will be a tool for serving wider national interests.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So far, the DP and DC payments have been put into a common pool and are not earmarked for use of projects in the vicinity of the properties involved.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Going forward, would the Ministry consider ploughing the LBC back into the community most directly affected by the land development, such as re-zoning or an increase in plot ratio?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: While such developments enhance the value of the land itself, they are not always beneficial to the vicinity.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Disamenities may include heavier vehicular and human traffic, noise, pollution, obstruction of scenic views and so on.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The payments can be utilised for upgrading community infrastructure and town improvement works as a form of compensation to the community.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would the Minister elaborate under what circumstances valuation will be required and will SLA continue to review LBC rates as frequently as possible with IRAS?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Mandarin):   With reference to the third and fourth objectives in clause 5, what will be the role of the LBC, in view of our new priorities in land planning and development as set out in the Singapore Green Plan 2030?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In addition, would the payments collected be used to help reduce the amounts we need to borrow for future long-term national infrastructure projects?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How does the Ministry intend to use the LBC for productivity enhancements in the construction industry, especially during the challenging times we are facing today?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would the Minister provide some examples which can serve to enlighten SMEs in the construction sector on how they can tap upon the incentives in this Bill?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In English): I would like to conclude with my support for the Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I will go straight into the queries that have been raised and try and address as many of them as I can.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Louis Ng, and I think Mr Louis Chua and Mr Leon Perera, asked about the concessionary relief.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Ng, in particular, asked what the planning objectives are that we intend to achieve by the grant of relief in section 13.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It will also make provision for future concessionary reliefs for developments that promote sustainable development of land and which balances the interest of current and future generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: An example of the continued provision for concessionary relief for change of use proposals within conserved buildings to incentivise the restoration of conserved buildings – I think a point that Mr Perera also touched on – and the adaptive reuse of conserved buildings.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is necessary to promote more optimal use of land, whilst at the same time, maintaining Singapore's cultural heritage.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Wee also asked for examples of concessionary relief to encourage construction productivity.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Any future relief schemes will be gazetted according to purposes and objectives set out in section 13 of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Appropriate measures will be considered to ensure that these objectives, as we have set out in this Bill for the new relief schemes will be achieved.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: MND will share more about this when they are ready.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Wee asked about the use of the LBC collections – I think Mr Chua did as well and so did Mr Ng – and whether LBC collections will reduce the amount of future borrowing needed for long-term national infrastructure projects.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As I mentioned at the outset, the existing framework is preserved, it is just put under one collection agency, and the LBC will be the name used for all three converted into LBC.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The consolidation is therefore not expected to result in a marked increase in the amount of revenue.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Indeed, the revenue to be collected will, of course, depend on the extent to which developers and landowners make an application for enhancement or intensification which triggers the use of LBC.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The LBC would thus be a part of the public monies available for this House for appropriate expenditures that benefit Singaporeans as a whole.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It would not be earmarked specifically for one purpose or one project, but it will be available generally, in the fund to benefit Singaporeans as a whole.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And, these, Mr Speaker, would include the funding of infrastructure, services and public programmes, including projects that benefit the local community, as well as broader national ones, such as the Singapore Green Plan.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For major infrastructure spend that is critical to Singapore's development, we have just talked about the SINGA Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This would smoothen hefty costs, which could run into tens of billions of dollars.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: By doing so, we will no longer need to pay for the costs upfront from our operating revenues.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is part of the Government's differentiated financing strategy for different types of expenditure.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Louis Ng asked whether the Minister's power to grant general exemptions will be exercised in line with the purposes of the Act; Mr Perera, and I think Mr Chua also did.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The short answer is yes; that is set out in section 5.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Ng may also wish to note that sections 12 and 13 require that every order made to grant an exemption or provide for concessionary relief must be presented in Parliament as soon as possible after publication in the Gazette.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Members of this House will be directly informed of the making of these exemptions when these are made.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think Mr Chua also made a point about this.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Ng asked how the Government will recover the benefits accrued by developers from unlawful development of land.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The purpose of the LBC Bill is to impose a tax on the increase in the value of land arising from a chargeable consent.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For unlawful developments involving a breach of planning control, URA under the Planning Act today may issue an enforcement notice.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The notice may require the removal of any unlawful structures and reinstatement of the land to its former site.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Don Wee asked whether SLA will continue to review the Table of Rates every six months with IRAS.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Yes, it will be reviewed to ensure that it continues to be updated and the circumstances under which the assessment of LBC by valuation is required.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That is similar to what is done for the DC Table of Rates today.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, as I said, the framework does not differ.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To Mr Perera's question, as to whether there will be a wholly new system, the answer, I think, is quite clear from what I said at the outset, and also my last statement that no, it would not be a wholly new system.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It will be similar to the existing framework.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In fact, it is a consolidation of the existing framework, which is why we felt that no public consultation was necessary in this case.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Valuations are required in specific circumstances, where the Table of Rates might not be applicable in circumstances, which I outlined earlier, such as, for unique developments, like for example, golf courses, theme parks, where there might not be a suitable or comparable use group or sufficiently rich source of data available.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Taxable persons might also opt to use LBC by valuation in lieu of the Table of Rates.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Perera might wish to know that this system of having a valuer as an option, apart from the Chief Valuer, currently is already available.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And there has not been any specific difficulty associated with that.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Murali asked if the DP system will continue outside the lifting of restrictive covenants.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And I think, specifically Mr Murali cited the example of remnant land parcels, odd pieces of land, which could be put together and developed upon.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Murali's point is that these odd pieces by themselves are not capable of independent development, but with amalgamation, they may have the potential to bring about enhancement.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Landowners who wish to purchase remnant state land will continue to have to pay a land premium as consideration to SLA for the remnant land parcel, and the LBC applicable for any chargeable consent thereafter granted on their private land parcel as a result of the amalgamation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, I think to answer Mr Murali's point, if you decide to put together the parcels and you need a chargeable consent to be given in respect of say, a restrictive covenant to be lifted, then an LBC will be levied.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Murali also asked for the Government's position on the applicability of the LBC in relation to Court decisions, citing examples such as the lifting of easements or restrictions, dominant/servient, tenement, for example, which may result in land value.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: A Court's decision to vary an easement or restriction would not in itself constitute a chargeable consent.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, in itself, it is not a chargeable consent, under the LBC Act.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, if you have a piece of land and you are subject to a Court decision – where the Court rules one way or another on the construction of the easement, for example, that itself will not amount to a chargeable consent.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: What the Court does is make a pronouncement as to the proper construction of the easement already existing as to what it should entail.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But having said that, it can certainly affect the value of the land and I think that is Mr Murali's point.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And this will certainly be taken on board in a valuation, should chargeable consent by the state be granted subsequently with respect to this piece of land with the Court's decision taken into account.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, the Court decision per se on itself, it would not be a chargeable consent, but if subsequently, in the context of the decision taken by the Court to vary or lift or otherwise construe a restriction in a positive manner, that will be taken into account as an enhancement in the land value.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In other words, if you develop ways not related to the land, the LBC is not designed to cream-off those appreciations.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In keeping with the principle in clause 5, that those who benefit financially when permission to develop the land is given should share some of that gain with the community.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And I think that is also a point raised by almost all the Members who spoke on this point.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Perera raised several specific questions and I will just address them here very quickly.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On the question of an IPC, I think Mr Perera's point is some might not be registered as a charity.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, it might be a society with an IPC status.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The regulations will consider this and will take this into account, even if you are not registered as a charity but have IPC status.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In relation to the renewal of leases, leasehold interest for state leases, a lease renewal premium is paid, not the LBC.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In terms of the LBC between the landlord and tenant, I think both Mr Chua and Mr Perera raised this, yes, it is collectible from the parties who have a material interest and that includes, in the context of a landlord and tenant, the tenant itself.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The tenant may have recourse to the landlord for any portion that the landlord ought to bear, but the provisions here set out the mechanism by which the state is able to levy the LBC as against any persons with an interest in the land.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And as Members would know, that includes the tenant.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To Mr Chua's point, if there is a dispute as to the valuation or disputes as to the way in which the Table of Rates is used, that dispute is taken to the Minister whose decision would be final.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On Mr Perera's question, as to whether there can be a deferment if one cannot pay the LBC.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Well, in the context of most cases, LBC is levied in a situation where there is an enhancement in the value of land.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, typically, a landowner or developer who obviously would have done his sums would come, make a proposal want to develop a piece of land, and obviously the intention behind that development is enhancement of land value.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Such a situation would not often arise, but should it arise, that is something that can be taken into account, as a matter of discretion.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And you look at the entire context of the situation in considering the appropriate deferment, if any.
